articleTitle: PQ, reliability and DG
abstract: DISTRIBUTED GENERATION (DG) CAN improve a utility's ability to serve peak load on a feeder, thus allowing the deferral of capital investments on a feeder. A common case where DG is effective and economical occurs when it helps to supply load during contingencies until the utility can build additional delivery capacity. Figure 1 shows an example with the DG located near the end of the feeder. In this location, DG can provide voltage support and reduce currents in the conductors near the substation [!}. Depending on the voltage and current constraints, the DG may even provide a larger increase in feeder capacity than the DG power rating. On the other hand, DG located near the substation might augment the capacity of the substation transformer or transmission system, but it does nothing to increase capacity on the feeder.

articleTitle: Flywheel UPS
abstract: ELECTRIC POWER QUALITY (PQ) HAS become an economic issue For end-users. Poor PQ can destroy the competitiveness of a company, especially companies in industries with narrow margins.

articleTitle: StatCom-SMES
abstract: SUPERCONDUCTING MAGNETIC energy storage (SMES) systems for power utility applications have received considerable attention due to their characteristics, such as rapid response (milliseconds), high power (multimegawatts), high efficiency, and four-quadrant control. SMES systems can provide improved system reliability, dynamic stability, enhanced power quality, and area protection [l]-[7], as its potential applications are summarized in Fig. 1 [7]. The squared area indicates the possible cost-effectiveness of SMES applications. Advances in both superconducting technologies and the necessary power electronics interface have made SMES a viable technology that can offer flexible, reliable, and fast-acting power compensation.

articleTitle: Breaking the ice [transmission line icing]
abstract: ICING OF POWER TRANSMISSION lines during winter storms is a persistent problem that causes outages and costs millions of dollars in repair expenses. High-frequency excitation at approximately 8-200 kHz has been proposed as a method to melt ice [1], [2]. The method works by a combination of two mechanisms. At these frequencies, ice is a lossy dielectric, causing heating directly in the ice. In addition, skin effect causes current to flow only in a thin layer on the surface of the line, causing resistive losses and consequent heating.

articleTitle: Small-scale hydropower
abstract: Large-scale hydroelectrical developments have become more and more difficult in many industrialized countries because of the shortage of undeveloped suitable sites and global environmental protection. However, there remain many sites suitable for small-scale hydroelectrical developments where “small-scale” denotes a power range from a few megawatts downward; for example, in Japan, approximately 2,400 potential sites remain.

articleTitle: Smaller is better? [micromotors and electric drives]
abstract: OVER 100 YEARS OF DESIGN AND analysis of electric machinery has been accomplished by those specializing in power systems, machinery, power electronics, and motor drives [1]. In the last decade, micromachining technology has enabled the use of small sensors and actuators in microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) [2], One category of actuators is the micromotor—an electric motor with a diameter on the order of 1 mm (different criteria can apply). Most work in this field is by semiconductor-fabrication specialists who generally do not have expertise in machine design and control. This article gives a perspective on micromotors from the vantage point of the electric drive specialty.

articleTitle: Gen-sets
abstract: EXISTING MILITARY GENERATOR sets (gen-sets) in the medium power range have been designed to be extremely rugged, cost-effective sources of power. These units are significantly heavier than their industrial counterparts to meet the stringent ruggedness requirements of the military and because the units provide additional features and capabilities that are not available on industrial units.

articleTitle: Reliability methods applied to The IEEE Gold Book Standard Network
abstract: The U.S. ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS power reliability enhancement program sponsored a survey effort to determine the various reliability/availability (R/A) analysis software tools available for utility, commercial, and industrial electrical and mechanical R/A analysis. The research quickly indicated that many users were utilizing a wide variety of analysis tools and techniques with different results. Many reliability models calculate only the reliability of load points within an industrial and commercial power system and fail to address the key indices required by industry, namely, reliability and annual down time at of load points and the frequency and duration of load point interruptions. Although many users were using different analysis techniques, the only recommended methodology presented in IEEE Standard 493, The IEEE Gold Book, since 1980 was the “series and parallel” reliability methodology and the “minimal cut-set method" that estimated the frequency and duration of load point interruptions.

articleTitle: No-load versus load loss
abstract: THE THEORY OF TRANSFORMER losses expressed as no-load loss and load loss is briefly reviewed in this article. Mathematical expressions for per-unit loss as a function of load are developed based on rated and actual load. Present value (PV) equations are used to express the cost of losses as a function of transformer characteristics, electricity cost, and discount rate. Three methods are presented for expressing the cost of losses in forms that can be used to evaluate bids.

articleTitle: Surge transference through transformers
abstract: A DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM CAN BE subjected to transient overvoltages due to surges of atmospheric origin transferred through the utility tie transformer, especially if it is of high turns ratio, i.e., the utility system voltage is high. Primary (high-voltage side) surge protection of the utility tie transformers is invariably provided. Secondary (low-voltage side) protection is also gaining momentum, though it may not be always provided in distribution systems. IEEE standard C62.41 [1] details the categories of secondary protection devices and contains recommendations for specific installations. The IEEE standard C62.22 [2] covers the application of metal oxide surge arresters in ac systems.

articleTitle: What's the real cost of higher efficiency? [electrical energy efficiency]
abstract: THE PROBLEMS THAT CALIFORNIA had with electrical energy last year have only emphasized the need to look at the true cost of high-efficiency energy devices used by cement plants since electrical energy is among the top expenses in producing cement. This article focuses on low-voltage induction motors and lighting systems. Low-voltage induction motors generally account for about 30% of the electrical energy consumed by a cement plant. Lighting systems generally account for about 3–5% of the electrical energy consumed by a cement plant, but it is a fixed load that does not directly contribute to production. Life-cycle cost analysis is used to determine the true costs of this equipment.

articleTitle: Watch the birdie! [overhead line faults]
abstract: AS SOCIETY BECOMES INCREASINGLY reliant on digital circuitry for hundreds of everyday uses, the importance of high-quality electrical power is becoming increasingly important for the global economy. With this shift to a digital society, business has become increasingly sensitive to disturbances in power supply. A recent study commissioned by the Electric Power Research Institute's (EPRI's) Consortium for Electric Infrastructure for a Digital Society (CEIDS) estimated that power-quality phenomena (voltage sags, surges, transients, and all other deviations from perfect power) are costing the U.S. economy between US$15 and 25 billion per year across all sectors [1].

articleTitle: Pull a few strings [complete protection of multistring fuseless capacitor banks]
abstract: THE TREND TOWARDS LARGE, fuseless shunt capacitor banks being employed in power systems is due to their lower cost, compact design, higher reliability with less exposed live parts, and lower losses. This article describes a novel application of the impedance method to provide complete bank protection by measuring the impedance of each series string of the capacitor bank. The scheme can identify the string(s) with an alarm or trip condition, keep the bank in service with pack failures in multiple strings, and trip only when the bank is actually in an unacceptable operating condition. Because this scheme can account for the distributed failure of packs in strings, bank availability can be increased.

articleTitle: Covering all the bases - industrial power system design in a utility environment
abstract: TYPICALLY, LARGE LOADS ASSOCIATED with petroleum distribution systems are located in a relatively confined plant area. Scattered distribution systems do not often have very large capacity. The combination of large industrial requirements coupled with the geographic requirements of a utility system calls for a challenging design.

articleTitle: HEV S/G [hybrid electric vehicle starter/generator]
abstract: EFFICIENT OPERATION OF INDUCTION I motor starter/alternator systems is an important part of the power-management function that is required in the self-contained vehicular environment. However, the nonlinear dynamics of the induction motor [ 1 ], parameter sensitivity to environmental factors, load complexities, and vehicular performance requirements make it difficult to determine and sustain the most efficient operating points. This article characterizes the performance of a fuzzy-logic controller for a hybrid electric vehicle (HEV) starter/generator (S/G) that is used to maintain optimum efficiency operation under both steady-state and dynamic-loading conditions. In steady-state conditions, automatic mapping of the maximum-efficiency operating points is achieved. Based on this data, the maximum possible efficiency under dynamic load profiling can be determined. In-vehicle dynamic loading is then emulated in the laboratory using a motor-development platform that can replay industry standard FTP75 road profiles and apply them to the S/G. The effects of velocity transients and the bandwidth of the fuzzy controller on efficiency are presented. The effectiveness of the fuzzy controller in maintaining high-efficiency operation and in reduced heating is demonstrated.

articleTitle: STS and induction motors
abstract: TRANSFER SYSTEMS USING mechanical switches have been applied for years in industrial plants as an effective counter-measure against long interruptions. By activating the transfer system when a second independent power source is available, the load can be transferred to the alternative source in a time ranging from around six cycles (for fast transfer schemes) to more than 36 cycles (for slow transfer, residual voltage transfer, or in-phase transfer schemes) [1].

articleTitle: Close contact [cross cutters, knives]
abstract: CROSS CUTTERS (CUTTER KNIVES) ARE used for the processing of endless pasteboards, cardboards, and plastic foils. The basic principle of a cross cutter is shown in Figure 1. In the paper industry, most cross cutters are synchronous cutters, i.e., cross cutters driven at synchronous speed where the length of the web cutoff is defined by the circumference described by a single rotation of the cross-cutter cylinders. These are used in the fine paper industry in machines called “cut size sheeters” and in the pulp industry as “cutter layboys.” Asynchronous cutters' knives (discussed in this article) are mainly used today in the corrugating industry and in so-called “folio sheeters.”

articleTitle: Benchmarking safety
abstract: ALL OF GENERAL INDUSTRY IN THE United States, represented by the participants in the IEEE/IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Committee Technical Conference (PCIC), is regulated by the federal government to have an electrical safety program. The Department of Labor's Occupational Safety and Health Administration's (OSHA) documents that drive the electrical safety of employees in the workplace is written in performance language.

articleTitle: AC induction motor specifications: an update on currently available procedures and options
abstract: THIS ARTICLE PROVIDES data for use in writing specifications for ac induction motors. Special attention will be given to motors used in the pulp and paper industries. Many modern materials and components are available that add to the reliability and life of electric motors. Also, newer designs are available that provide significant energy savings over the life of the machine.

articleTitle: The first electric power transmission line in North America-Oregon City, Oregon
abstract: In the 1800s, the development of the incandescent electric light bulb by Edison and others and the invention of dc and ac motors by Gramme and Tesla led to the commercial use of larger and larger amounts of electric power in the United States. Every year since, the demand for electric power has shown dramatic increases.

articleTitle: The arc terminator
abstract: THE CONTINUING EMPHASIS THAT is being placed upon worker safety has prompted a trend in the medium-voltage, metal-clad switchgear industry, requiring it to offer switchgear equipment that incorporates a capability for safely withstanding any open-arcing fault condition that may occur within any of the compartments. Today, because of this increased awareness of the arc-flash hazard, more companies are beginning to specify that switchgear enclosures be of the type known as “arc-resistant construction.”

articleTitle: All your eggs in one basket [back-up protection using multifunction relays]
abstract: MULTIFUNCTION MICROPROCESSOR based relays are commonly used in modern installations due to the many advantages they offer, such as communications, measurements, simplified wiring, self monitoring, and reduced space requirements. A reliable protection scheme is very important in order to protect capital equipment and operating personnel and reduce down time by selectively clearing faults. Back-up protection is also normally provided to ensure the elimination of faults should the primary protection circuit fail. In this article, the authors show how the features of modern multifunction relays can be used to enhance back-up protection.

articleTitle: The standards professional: the employee you didn't know you needed. I
abstract: While most companies today have a specific in dividual, perhaps even an entire organization, who is responsible for corporate objectives and oversight in quality, environmental issues, and safety, there seems to be a stigma attached to the same level of oversight for standards. In fact, most companies, though they may have dozens or even hundreds of employees participating in the standards community, still perceive “standards stuff” to be simply a technical contribution rather than the fundamental business issue it really is.

articleTitle: Light years [cathode heating effect on lamp life in dimming use]
abstract: THE AIM OF THE WORK DESCRIBED in this article is to find out the effect of cathode-heating voltage during continuous burning to the lamp life in dimming use. For a ballast manufacturer, it is important to know how the ballast affects lamp life when lamps are dimmed, for instance, according to daylight. On days when there is plenty of daylight, lamps are dimmed on low light levels for long periods. With optimum cathode heating provided by the electronic ballast, lamp life is prolonged.

articleTitle: Renovation for more reliability [oil refinery power system upgrade]
abstract: PARAGUANA REFINING CENTER (CRP) in Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) is the largest oil-refining complex in the world, with a distillation capacity of 900,000 bbl/d. It is located in the Paraguana Peninsula, Falcon State, Venezuela. CRP services two large refineries: Amuay and Cardon. Amuay capacity is 640,000 bbl/d. Currently, Amuay's daily average electric consumption is about 121 MW; 107 MW are associated to process loads, and 14 MW are for the residential area and refinery offices. The refinery has an installed generating capacity of 182 MW; 84 MW are based in gas turbines, and 98 MW in steam turbines. There are four gas turbogenerators (TGs) and seven steam TGs (Figs. 1 and 2).

articleTitle: Rediscovering William Stanley, Jr. Part I
abstract: William Stanley, Jr. pioneered the development and use of ac for electric light and power applications. He conceived solutions before others recognized the problems. He contributed in a major way to a major invention: the transformer, the key to large-scale exploitation of ac electricity. Prior to 1885, few people were interested in ac except as a way to circumvent problems with sparking commutators on rotating electric machines. In March 1886, Stanley demonstrated a system of single-phase ac for lighting applications in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, that changed the worldview of electricity. His system showcased the transformer that he had invented two years before. For the first time, this demonstration of long-distance, step-up/step-down, ac power transmission brought into public view the significant benefits offered by ac over dc. Stanley led the way as engineers worldwide extended power transmission to ever higher potentials and increasing distances. He also invented an inductor electric machine that was widely used as an alternator prior to 1900.

articleTitle: Georg Simon Ohm (of Ohm's law)
abstract: Georg Simon Ohm was a famous German scientist in the 19th century. His name was probably spoken more often than any other scientific name by electrical engineers during the Romantic Era of Electrical Engineering (before personal computers).

articleTitle: Continuing journeys in arc-flash injury prevention: IEEE standard 1584
abstract: On the July/August 2002 issue of this column, I noted that, for more than 20 years, IAS members have been at the forefront in advancing science and technology to better understand the arc-flash phenomena and applying this knowledge in the evolution of technologies, regulations, standards, products, and work practices to reduce the risk of injuries from the arc-flash hazard. Another significant chapter in this body of knowledge was completed in 2002 with the publication of the first edition of IEEE Standard 1584, Guide for Performing Arc Flash Calculations. This guide is now available for use in performing arc-flash hazard analysis studies and determining potential thermal incident energy exposure for people working on or near electrical equipment.

articleTitle: Spot, don't bump
abstract: High-power, line-fed, constant-speed motors must sometimes be operated at very low speed for controlled positioning of the attached load equipment. This process is referred to as “spotting” or “inching.” Examples include cement-grinding mills (both raw and finish) and metal-processing rolls. These motors are usually medium voltage (more than 2,300 V). Two methods of spotting motors have been used in the past: bumping the motor with the medium-voltage motor starter and spotting with an electromechanical inverter. This article describes the application of a low voltage (460-V output) pulsewidth modulated (PWM) adjustable-speed drive to medium- voltage motors for spotting purposes. The drive is capable of rotating a synchronous or induction motor at low speed under manual control to position the machine attached to the motor to a desired position.

articleTitle: The heart and soul of your electrical safety culture
abstract: Why would you use electrical case histories, and why would you bother to share them? It takes time, effort, and resources to investigate and implement findings. Is it worth all the trouble? Sometimes described as lessons learned, or in the Nuclear Power Industry as operating experience (OPEX), they are now recognized as the prime drivers of safer work and, correspondingly, more productive business units. They are now an integral part of day-to-day business in nuclear power plants, and OPEX is discussed and built into each and every task.

articleTitle: Edith Clarke and power system stability
abstract: [This article originally appeared in “Scanning the Past” in the January 1996 issue »/Proceedings of the IEEE.] In 1941, Edith Clarke and Seldon B. Crary presented a joint paper on stability problems in power engineering at a meeting of the America Institute of Electrical Engineering (AIEE) in Philadelphia. At the time, Clarke and Crary were both employed as engineers by the General Electric Company (GE), and their paper received a prize as the best paper published that year. Clarke had overcome many difficulties on her way to becoming a highly respected member of the electrical engineering profession. She specialized in the analysis of electric power systems and devoted her career to the simplification and mechanization of problem solving in that field.

articleTitle: Line breaking failure
abstract: OVERHEAD POWER LINES OCCASIONALLY fail structurally (break) and fall to the ground where they can be a significant danger. The causes for line failure are many and represent a safety concern recognized by the National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) and electrical utilities.

articleTitle: "Applied" science [ICEA medium voltage power cable specifications]
abstract: THE INSULATED I Cable Engineers Association (ICEA) has recently issued new standards, published by the National Electric Manufacturing Association (NEMA) for solid-dielectric insulated power cables. These new standards are: □ ICEA S-95-658-1999/NEMA WC70, Standard for Nonshielded Power Cables Rated 2000 Volts or Less for the Distribution of Electrical Energy [1] □ ICEA S-96-659-1999/NEMA WC 71, Nonshielded Power Cables Rated 2001-5000 Volts for the Distribution of Electrical Energy [2] □ ICEA S-93-639-2000/NEMA WC 74, 5–46 kV Shielded Power Cable for Use in the Transmission and Distribution of Electric Energy [3].

articleTitle: A second chance
abstract: I never expected to write a column like this, but I have had a life-changing experience. In early April of this year, I attended the IEEE Panel of Editors Meeting in Washington, DC. After a very tiring first day, I returned to my hotel room to be greeted by my wife, daughter, and son-in-law. They asked how I was feeling, and I said, “Not great.” They responded, “It is time to go to the hospital,” which we did after I made some minor protests.

articleTitle: The standards professional: the employee you didn't know you needed. II
abstract: How companies organize their standards activities to address strategic standards management (SSM) varies widely from tightly centralized control to no control at all. This is largely dependent on the history and culture of the organization and, to a lesser extent, on the industry it supports. But, regardless of the organizational structure, the two basic management functions of SSM (internal standards oversight and long-term strategic commitment) are made significantly easier to implement if the company has a dedicated individual (or two) responsible for corporate-level concerns in the area of standards: the standards professional.

articleTitle: Accidents always happen to the "other guy"!
abstract: A few months ago, while my wife Cindy was visiting her mom and dad, I suffered a nasty fall from the roof of our two-story home, landing in our front yard. We live on a cul-de-sac with six houses on our street, so there is no through traffic, and, like most of us today, our neighbors live in the rear of their houses. I was conscious after the fall and tried calling for help without much success. To my surprise, Bernie came running over within seconds of my fall, screaming “Don't move, I've called 911 and they will be here shortly!" Bernie, who lives across the street, happened to be looking out of his bedroom window and saw me fall. The arrival of the ambulance brought out the rest of our neighbors, and soon each knew the seriousness of my condition. The EMTs immobilized me, placed me on a “board," took me to the nearest heliport, and I was “life flighted” toa Pittsburgh hospital. One of our neighbors contacted Cindy, and she arrived at the hospital to find me in the trauma unit of the emergency room. I was still conscious when we learned that I had broken vertebra in my back, five broken ribs, and internal bleeding.

articleTitle: IAS standards development - A comparison
abstract: Previous articles in this column discussed the importance of standards to employers, industry, individuals, and society. The IEEE is one of the foremost standards development organizations (SDOs) in North America and the rest of the world. IEEE standards cover many areas of technology, including computers, communications, radio-frequency interference, electric power systems and components, and many facets of industrial applications. These standards help provide stability to an industry as well as a level playing field for all the players in a competitive environment.

articleTitle: Out of our imagination - electrical safety in the 25th century
abstract: Rather than be satisfied with small incremental change as weeks pass to months, let's consider a vast break with the “now” of electrical safety and imagine a 25th century future. What could be done in the 25th century? From the movie Star Trek: First Contact, written by Berman, Braga, and Moore (1997), we can listen to Captain Picard: “… The economics of the future are somewhat different. You see, money doesn't exist in the 24th century…. The acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force in our lives. We work to better ourselves and the rest of humanity.”

articleTitle: Jumpin' jazz [low voltage power system]
abstract: THIS ARTICLE DESCRIBES THE OPERATE and maintenance of a low-voltage power s tern used to power a jazz café. This is not necessarily an important factor in the natio economy, but problems encountered and described herein may be representative of many small commercial operations, such as restaurants, grocery stores, drug stores, and similar sized shops. When engineers consider the design for commercial operations, the thought is generally on high-rise type office buildings or some similar facility [1]. What is important to remember is that, while there are probably more small installations than large capacity systems, the small shops do not normally have a maintenance crew for support. After reading this article, one should be left with the thought that we have a gap to fill. For this article, the term “café” will be used, even though it is not purely descriptive.

articleTitle: Elena Schreiber: from RN to electrical engineer
abstract: [This article originally appeared in “Scanning the Past” in the January 1996 issue »/Proceedings of the IEEE.] In 1941, Edith Clarke and Seldon B. Crary presented a joint paper on stability problems in power engineering at a meeting of the America Institute of Electrical Engineering (AIEE) in Philadelphia. At the time, Clarke and Crary were both employed as engineers by the General Electric Company (GE), and their paper received a prize as the best paper published that year. Clarke had overcome many difficulties on her way to becoming a highly respected member of the electrical engineering profession. She specialized in the analysis of electric power systems and devoted her career to the simplification and mechanization of problem solving in that field.

articleTitle: Memory motors
abstract: A NEW CLASS OF PERMANENT-MAGNET (PM) machines, named memory motors for their ability to change the intensity of magnetization and memorize the flux density level in rotor magnets is described in the article. A memory motor can be built either as a variable-flux or pole-changing machine. In both machine types, the magnetization of PMs can be simply varied by a short current pulse, with no need for permanent demagnetizing current as in conventional internal PM machines at flux-weakening mode. The demagnetizing current flows through stator winding(s) supplied from the same source as the stator current. Memory motors combine advantages of a wound-rotor machine (variable rotor flux) with those of a wide-speed machine (no excitation losses), resulting in a unique machine concept that has the potential to find numerous applications in electric drives.

articleTitle: Motor winding problems caused by inverter drives
abstract: FOR OVER 70 YEARS, RESEARCHERS have understood that fast rise-time voltage surges from a circuit breaker closing can lead to an electrical breakdown of the turn insulation in motor stator windings [1]. If the turn insulation is of an insufficient thickness or has aged in service, the insulation will puncture when a short rise-time voltage surge occurs. Punctured turn insulation allows for a very high circulating current to flow into the affected copper turn, rapidly melting the copper conductors, which, in turn, results in a consequent burning/melting of the slot liner insulation, thus leading to a stator winding ground fault [2], [3].

articleTitle: Neutral shift [five years of continuous operation with adjustable frequency drives]
abstract: IN 1998, A LARGE MIDWESTERN refinery undercook a US$150 million project to update and optimize a 50,000-bbl/d fluidized-bed catalytic cracking unit (FCCU). The FCCU is one of the most important units within a refinery and is the largest producing unit of high-octane gasoline blend stock. The scope of the project included a complete replacement of the FCCU reactor, combustion air compressor, wet gas compressor, and the addition of a flue gas scrubber to reduce particulate emissions. The FCCU portion of the project was completed during a planned refinery maintenance turnaround in November 2000. A companion project to construct a new gas plant for an existing 25,000-bbl/d Coker unit was completed in May 2001. This article will discuss the FCC and Coker wet gas compressors. The project was justified on the basis of energy conservation, improved product yield, reduced maintenance costs, improved reliability, and environmental compliance. Much of the energy savings were expected to be realized through efficiency improvements in the combustion air and wet gas compressors. The existing FCCU was a steam turbine driven centrifugal compressor that operated at approximately 65% efficiency. An electric driver was chosen due to the lower maintenance cost versus a steam turbine. Since the refinery must typically purchase natural gas to supplement internally produced gas to make steam, the cost of steam was higher than the cost of electricity on a per-horsepower basis. As is typical of the refining industry, an interruption of either of these critical units would shut down or severely curtail the entire process and cost millions of dollars in lost production. Hence, total process reliability was of prime importance in making equipment selections.

articleTitle: SCADA and IP: is network convergence really here?
abstract: Convergence is a term that HAS received a great deal of airtime in recent years. Vendors, consultants, and industry pundits have been preaching for some time about the benefits to be derived from networks that support multiple services. While much of chat discussion has been somewhat subjective and vaporous in the past, recent developments in applications for Internet protocol (IP) enabled networks have made convergence an achievable, real-world goal.

articleTitle: Be prepared! [power industry deregulation]
abstract: THE CALIFORNIA ENERGY CRISIS HAS brought electric power deregulation to the forefront for electricity users in the United States. Could what happened in California occur in other states? Process industries are asking themselves what they can do to prepare for the consequences of electric power deregulation in the United States. This article will give manufacturers an overview of the current electric power industry and the trends in that industry. The article will then discuss concerns about deregulation and outline different options that users might consider to address their concerns.

articleTitle: Mind your P's and Q's [power-quality events capture, data acquisition system]
abstract: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS AGO, CAPTURING multiple channels of simultaneous data required multiple oscilloscopes or a very specialized, expensive, and customized data-acquisition system. In order to capture power-quality (PQ) events, very sophisticated methods were used to invoke simultaneous triggering across all recording channels. Normally, triggering was accomplished using overvoltage or overcurrent conditions, and, typically, you only had one shot—imagine having to ask the utility company, “Can you switch that 36-Mvar capacitor bank again, I missed the trigger?” In addition, there was no easy way to get an oscilloscope to trigger on an undervoltage event (like a sag, for example). Today, all of that has changed; we are now able to record multiple channels of simultaneous data using many types of triggering mechanisms. This article will discuss the evolution of triggering PQ instrumentation and the advanced triggering systems available for portable and fixed panel-mounted meters.

articleTitle: In SYNC [synchronising applications with MV drives]
abstract: Pumps or fans often exist in multiples or configurations that are interdependent within a process. Without applying a drive to each unit, it is still possible to achieve the benefits of drive control by taking advantage of synchronization and using one drive to control several pumps within a process. Several benefits may be realized while keeping capital outlays reasonable. Possible applications must be identified and evaluated separately to ensure economic payback and benefits. The method and configuration chosen will impact the evaluation.

articleTitle: Earthing or grounding?
abstract: Grounding strongly affects personnel safety, equipment safety and operation, power distribution systems, solid-state systems and computers, and static- and lightning-protection systems. Improper earthing-grounding installations can result in equipment damage or improper operation, especially in solid-state equipment. Improper earthing-grounding systems can result in not only electrical injures and shocks, but may have also resulted in electrocution. Many of the misconceptions with today's grounding systems will be disclosed and corrective action will be offered.

articleTitle: Selecting ASD systems
abstract: FOR OVER 100 YEARS, THE THREE-PHASE I ac induction motor has proven to be an extremely reliable electromechanical conversion device. For the vast majority of that period, it evolved as a constant speed device operating from a constant frequency, constant voltage, and sinusoidal utility power source. Its characteristics are well defined and standardized in this mode of operation by the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

articleTitle: Lifelong education
abstract: THE NEED TO UNDERSTAND THAT hazards associated with electrical energy are dangerous and essentially invisible begins with early childhood development and continues throughout adulthood. The presence of an electrical hazard can only be seen by observing signals and signs of its presence. In order to avoid a hazard, a person must either be trained to recognize signs of the hazard's presence or a knowledgeable person must devise a mechanism to afford the necessary protection. Of course, depending upon someone else to point out a hazard is much less effective than personally understanding the hazard. All people who use electrical energy are exposed to an electrical hazard to some degree.

articleTitle: Vdc takes on Vac [system control voltage selection]
abstract: IN THE PAST, CONTROL DEVICES have required coo much power to make 24 Vdc products cost effective or practical. During the past few years, industrial-control product manufacturers have placed more emphasis on 24 Vdc as the control voltage of choice. Design innovations, like increased microprocessor content and separation of control and power circuits, have reduced control-power requirements. The result has been dc power supplies with improved reliability at reduced costs. Technology advances in power-transistor ampere ratings have helped reduce the issues of excessive dc voltage drop over long cable runs. This has led to an increase in the variety of 24-Vdc-controlled devices along with improvements in quality, robustness, features, and size.

articleTitle: Benefits of upgrading: paper mill generator protection
abstract: ELECTRICAL GENERATION AT PAPER mills is becoming an increasingly critical asset and should be well protected from faults, system upsets and abnormal operating conditions. The loss of a major generating unit for an extended period would result in very costly replacement power and repair costs for any paper mill. This article presents the reasons why mill generator owners should consider upgrading the electrical protection of their generators to meet today's standards. It specifically outlines the risks assumed in protection areas where 20-year-old (and older) generator protection is inadequate. The article relates the experience of completed protection upgrade projects at MeadWestvaco's Luke Mill in Maryland, USA, where 1960-vintage electromechanical relays were replaced with modern digital protection. This article points out the advantages of this technology versus conventional electromechanical protection and also discusses the unique application considerations in applying digital protection.

articleTitle: One company's approach to cord-connected safety
abstract: IN ANY LARGE MANUFACTURING facility, there exists an inherent danger that is easy to overlook yet may be the most significant electrocution hazard to employees who work daily in the process, manufacturing, or fabrication areas. Cord-connected electrical equipment, with voltages ranging from 120–480 Vac, is often taken for granted and may be routinely moved around the plant and plugged in. Assumptions about the electrical safety of using this equipment are often based on the fact that the particular cord-connected equipment, or other similar equipment, has been used in such a manner for many years without incident. The condition of the cord and of the actual equipment may be overlooked because “as long as I can remember it's looked like that.”

articleTitle: From DC to AC [rotary lime kiln conversion]
abstract: THIS ARTICLE PRESENTS A CASE history of the conversion of a rotary lime kiln from a dc drive system to an ac drive system. The discussion includes the following aspects: □ existing equipment and its history □ the need for the upgrade and the required results □ mechanical drive-line considerations □ drive alternatives investigated □ a description of the hardware used □ the installation □ drive commissioning □ results achieved □ future enhancements.

articleTitle: Get in the zone! [zone equipment installation]
abstract: THE METHODS OF PROTECTING I classified locations that have been commonly used in the United States are explosionproof, purged and pressurized, and intrinsic safety. These methods of protection have been well adapted to the Division method of classification used in the United States and Canada, with sufficient products available to support them. Hermetic sealing, oil-immersion, and nonincendive methods are also allowed by Article 501 of the National Electrical Code (NEC) [1] for use in Class 1, Division 2 areas. The NEC and other standards and practices have been established and in force for a considerable length of time, providing support, definition, criteria, and regulation for the manufacture and installation of affected products and devices. Recent attempts to adapt the European International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) derived Zone method of classification and the methods of explosion protection developed for application in the Zone-rated installations in the United States have received mixed responses.

abstract: The chair of the 11th Annual IEEE IAS Electrical Safety Workshop, D. Ray Crow, extends his personal invitation for you to join him and several hundred electrical safety colleagues on 10-13 February 2004 at the Oakland Marriott Hotel in Oakland, California.

articleTitle: IEEE policies and procedures for standards development
abstract: In previous columns this year, we have discussed the need for standards and the standards vitality of the IAS (the IAS is the fourth largest creator of standards in the IEEE). This month's column will discuss the evolving structure in the IEEE standards development process.

articleTitle: The IEEE electrical safety resource center
abstract: At the 2002 IAS Electrical Safety Workshop in Biloxi, Mississippi, USA, a conversation between past Workshop Chair Kim Eastwood and IEEE Standards Association (SA) staff member Sue Vogel has resulted in a new resource in electrical safety. Kim was looking for a way to connect the multitude of electrical safety activities throughout the IEEE, and Sue wanted to create a Web portal into the various safety-related standards in the IEEE. The product of that conversation, and the subsequent time and energy they and others contributed to their vision, is the IEEE Electrical Safety Resource Center on the SA Web site. The Resource Center (http://standards.ieee.org/esrc) was officially launched in May 2003 as part of IEEE support of Electrical Safety Month and sponsored by the Electrical Safety Foundation International.

abstract: Our Society is continuing to be an active technology leader. Two major new initiatives within the IEEE have IAS participation and support.

abstract: Richard Hulett, a senior vice president of electrical products for Thermon Manufacturing Company in San Marcos, Texas, USA, has been elevated to the highest membership grade within the IEEE: Fellow.

abstract: This column will provide updates on two popular student programs for the 2003 IAS Annual Meeting to be held in Salt Lake City, Utah, USA. They are the Myron Zucker Design Contest and the Myron Zucker Student Travel Program.

articleTitle: The IEEE Richard Harold Kaufmann award
abstract: The Richard Harold Kaufmann Award is a part of the IEEE family of technical field awards. Concepts of the Kaufmann award were developed by myself, presented to the IAS Executive Board in 1986, and proposed that the IAS sponsor the award. It followed that the IEEE Richard Harold Kaufmann Award was established by the IEEE Board of Directors “for outstanding contributions in industrial systems engineering.”

articleTitle: 2002 RAB leadership award to Subrata Mukhopadhyay
abstract: IAS Member and present Delhi Joint-Chapter Chair Subrata Mukhopadhyay has been named as one of the three winners of the 2002 IEEE Regional Activities Board (RAB) Leadership Award. He was nominated by the Standing Committee on Awards and Fellow Nomination of the Delhi Section. The selection was made by the RAB Awards and Recognition Committee, and approval was given by the IEEE RAB. RAB has honored him with this award for the outstanding contributions he has made to numerous IEEE activities and the example he set in carrying forward the goals and objectives of IEEE RAB. His award citation reads “for sustained and dedicated technical and professional leadership to the IEEE Delhi Section and Region 10.” The award was presented to him during the IEEE Region 10 Meeting in April 2003 in Malaysia.

abstract: Maria Ines Castro Simas passed away on 8 August 2002, in Lisbon, Portugal. Her warm presence and competent leadership will be greatly missed by friends and associates in the IEEE/IAS. abstract: M. Dayne Aldridge, P. E., has been awarded the 2002 IEEE Educacional Activities Board (EAB) Meritorious Achievement A ward in Accreditation Activities. On 15 November at the EAB A wards Ceremony at the IEEE Board Series in Itasca, Illinois, USA, IEEE Vice President for EAB, Lyle Feisel, honored Mr. Aldridge's “outstanding contributions to the development and implementation of the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET) Engineering Criteria 2000 and the enhancement of the quality of engineering education.”

articleTitle: John B. Dwyer in memoriam
abstract: IAS Member Jack Dwyer passed away in January 2003. Jack was active in the IAS Petroleum and Chemical Industry Committee (PCIC) since 1964 and served as PCIC Membership Subcommittee Chair from 1977–2002. “Jack was a true gentleman; he was always in the background keeping the gears and cogs of PCIC well oiled and running smoothly,” stated Rick Bried, PCIC History Chair. Jack and his wife, Dolores, were known to most PCIC attendees as the hosts of an annual PCIC conference social event. Teaming together, they welcomed each guest with warmth and enthusiasm.

Rashid honored with IEEE EAB award in continuing education
abstract: In the last decade, Dr. Rashid has given more than 30 invited lectures and short courses from Dhaka, Bangladesh, to Perth, Australia, to Indiana, USA. “Technology reinvents itself every six to 12 months and waits for no one,” he said. “Those who keep up and constantly seek to expand their horizons ‘in whatever their field’ will have the best chances of getting ahead, working on their own, and switching careers whenever they choose. articleTitle: Nineteen IAS members achieve fellow status
abstract: Nineteen members of the IAS have achieved the highest honor of IEEE membership with their elevation to Fellow, effective 1 January 2003. The IEEE Board of Directors approved the selection of new Fellows after professional evaluations and reviews by societies and awards committees. Eight new Fellows were evaluated by the IAS Fellows Committee and 11 were selected by other societies. Congratulations to these new IEEE Fellows!

articleTitle: Petroleum and chemical industry committee conference awards luncheon
abstract: The 49th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Committee conference was held in New Orleans on 23 September 2002. Attending were 1,127 registrants and 499 guests. Tropical storm Isidore provided some excitement with a direct hit on New Orleans in the middle of the conference; however, most folks rode out the storm and were rewarded with great papers and networking with associates. The Monday Awards Luncheon provides the annual opportunity to recognize outstanding PCIC contributors and was attended this year by IEEE President Ray Findlay and IAS President Mark Nelms.

articleTitle: 2002 P.K. Sen senior design project award
abstract: The Industry Applications Society strongly encourages chapters to submit news items or articles for publication in the IAS magazine. It gives a chapter a great opportunity to publish in a journal that is read world wide, to promote and publicize activities to membership, and also to receive credit in the chapters awards process. This month we have two articles from chapters located at opposite sides of the world. From the Joint IAS/PES chapter in Denver, Colorado, USA, we have an article announcing the results of an annual award for senior design projects, and from the Joint IAS/PES chapter in Delhi, India, we have an article relating the Sixth Annual Thomas Alva Edison Memorial Lecture on “High Reliability Power System Design” given by PES Distinguished Lecturer Keene Masayuki Matsuda. We appreciate these chapters for taking the time to share these articles with us. It's always good to hear news from our chapters and we look forward to hearing from many more.

articleTitle: George W. Walsh in memoriam
abstract: The IAS has lost one of its most distinguished members. George W. Walsh, 79, of Glenville, New York, USA, died Tuesday, 11 March 2003, following a lengthy illness.

articleTitle: The IEEE EMERALD book
abstract: This column is devoted to a discussion of The IEEE Emerald Book. Officially, The IEEE Emerald Book is IEEE Standard 1100, IEEE Recommended Practice for Powering and Grounding Sensitive Electronic Equipment. The IEEE Emerald Book is moving through the periodic revision process under the leadership of Chris Melhorn (c.melhorn@ieee.org). If you are interested in participating in the development of The IEEE Emerald Book, feel free to contact chairperson Melhorn or, better yet, attend either the IAS Industrial and Commercial Power Systems conference (held each May) or the IAS Annual Meeting (held each October), get involved, and participate in person.

articleTitle: Curtis L. Ivey in Memoriam [1930-2003]
abstract: Curtis L. Ivey, longtime IEEE and IAS member, passed away on 17 February 2003 after a brief illness. Mr. Ivey was born in Pikesville, Kentucky, USA, on 2 April 1930, was raised in Ohio, and graduated from the University of Akron with a B.S.E.E. in 1953. He received the M.S.E.E. degree from the State University of New York at Buffalo in 1966. Curt, as he was known by his many friends and associates, served in the U.S. Army during the Korean conflict and became a member of the AIEE, the predecessor of the IEEE, in 1954. In 1960, he became an active member of the Pulp and Paper Committee and served as general chairman of its 1982 Technical Conference and as committee chairman in 1984-1985. He received the Meritorious Service Award of the committee. Curt became a member of the IAS Executive Board in 1985, when he was named the chairman of the Process Industries Department. In 1987, he was named chairman of the Administration Department and served in that position until January 1991 when he was elected to the office of treasurer. He served in this capacity until his professional retirement in 1994.
